reports.one_line: Not an equity IPO: SMCG04 is SMC Global's fourth public issue of secured, ICRA A (Stable) rated NCDs (₹75 cr base + ₹75 cr green shoe, ₹1,000 face value). It is a loan to a 30-year-old, mid-sized, promoter-run broking/insurance-broking/NBFC group whose credit is adequate but has been weakening: FY26 profit fell to ₹103 cr, gearing is rising and capital-market regulation has tightened. The final 2026 coupon and objects could not be verified from the prospectus itself.

This is not an equity IPO but a Rs.1 crore Zero Coupon Zero Principal (ZCZP) donation instrument on NSE's Social Stock Exchange for a Hyderabad cancer-screening charity: buyers get no interest, no principal back and nothing tradable, so it fails as an investment. It may be a reasonable 80G-eligible donation, but the charity's finances and project budget could not be checked against the offer document.

A Kolkata family-run imitation-jewellery wholesaler (City Girl / Manikya brands, about 82% wholesale, about 66% West Bengal) raising Rs 34.99 crore, all fresh issue, on NSE SME to move into in-house plating and B2C showrooms. Profits tripled in FY26 but operating cash flow was negative, inventory days tripled, the expansion has no orders placed and approvals are still pending, and there is no visible moat.

A five-year-old Gurugram MICE/incentive-travel organiser with ~₹100 cr of largely pass-through revenue, 86% of it from banking and insurance clients and 43% from a single customer, raising ₹38.12 cr (all fresh) mainly to fund a receivables build-up and repay debt; profits are rising, but cash flow is negative and the governance record is patchy. Avoid.

A four-year-old Surat maker of lab-grown-diamond (LGD) studded gold jewellery that mostly sells B2B. Revenue has grown fast (Rs.53.7 cr in FY24 to about Rs.203 cr in FY26), but operating cash flow has been negative for three straight years and customers and suppliers are highly concentrated. There is no clear moat in a crowded, deflating LGD market, and the Rs.108 cr fresh issue mainly pays for more working capital.

A Pune-based, family-run maker of railway PSC sleepers and site-fabricated MS/penstock pipes with a Rs 581.8 cr order book, but no real moat and a thick web of promoter-group dealings. Most of the Rs 145 cr fresh money goes to working capital and small debt paydown, and the issue has almost no institutional allocation (QIB capped at 1%), so retail investors are the price-setters.

A small Bikaner papad maker (FY26 revenue Rs 33.5 cr, PAT Rs 5.2 cr) whose reported profits have barely turned into cash: inventory is about 75% of annual sales. It has no real moat, runs parallel snack businesses on the promoter side, and nearly a third of the fresh money goes to paying down a revolving bank line. Avoid.

A 30-year-old, Gujarat-concentrated (96% of active clients) full-service retail broker raising Rs 90.17 cr of fresh money mostly for working capital. Revenue fell 24% and PAT 44% in FY26, active clients grew under 1%, there is no discernible moat, and a SEBI penalty over the handling of client funds in 2024-25 weighs on the governance record.

SRIT India is a Bengaluru government IT system integrator. About 89% of its revenue comes from tenders, it relies heavily on subcontractors, and its receivables are swelling. The Rs.218.4 cr all-fresh issue mostly funds working capital and unidentified acquisitions. Profit growth is real, but cash generation, concentration and the business model make this one to avoid.

A loss-making value e-commerce marketplace (Snapdeal) bundled with a profitable but only 26%-owned listed SaaS subsidiary (Unicommerce); most of the Rs 287 crore fresh issue goes to Snapdeal marketing and tech spend, the largest promoter (SoftBank's Starfish) is selling, and the issue qualified only under the loss-making-company route with 75% reserved for QIBs.

A Kolkata-based, tender-driven IT/network system integrator whose reported profits have jumped, but cash has not come in. Operating cash flow was negative in FY26, receivables run at 280 days, and the entire fresh issue goes to fund more working capital. Reported growth, no moat, weak cash conversion and a thin governance record: avoid.

reports.company: German Green Steel and Power Limited
reports.one_line: German Green Steel and Power is a Gujarat-focused maker of secondary-route TMT bars that is growing and fairly well run operationally. It is raising Rs.290 crore mostly for a sensible capacity expansion, but it has no real moat, 98% of its sales are in one state, it does not own its brand, and there are live governance issues: a Rs.112.65 crore income-tax contingent liability after a 2023 search, a web of promoter entities, and recent compliance penalties. We would avoid it for now.

A Haryana solar-pump EPC contractor that earns ~97% of revenue from state agencies under PM-KUSUM, now raising ~₹61 cr fresh (plus a ₹7.35 cr promoter OFS) mostly to fund receivables and a module-line expansion. Reported profits have jumped, but it has no real moat, operating cash flow has not followed profit, its main subsidy scheme's Phase I expired in March 2026, and the governance record has too many lapses.

A real, fast-growing maker of LAN, fibre and specialty cables with about 22% of India's networking-cable market, but growth has come with negative operating cash flow, a 7x rise in debt, heavy customer concentration and a live lawsuit over its own name. 42% of the issue is a promoter exit. Worth tracking, not buying at the IPO.

A Mumbai-focused, family-controlled residential developer with a large legacy land bank and rising pre-sales. It is raising Rs.500 crore, all fresh issue and mostly to repay debt, but still carries heavy leverage, has had negative operating cash flow in each of the last three years, and has related-party transactions that its own auditors flagged as prejudicial. Worth tracking, not applying.

A southern-India, backward-integrated secondary steel maker (sponge iron to TMT bars, coils and pipes) with a volatile, thin-margin earnings record, raising Rs 355 cr of fresh money mostly to repay debt, and carrying several governance flags from promoter-group dealings around its NCLT-acquired subsidiary Basai Steels.

A leveraged, trader-sourced shrimp and dried-chilli processor from Andhra Pradesh with growing profits but three straight years of negative operating cash flow, a China-heavy export book and a patchy compliance record, raising ₹53.1 crore mainly to double shrimp capacity in a plant that will not run until April 2028 while the current one is under-utilised: avoid.

India's largest digital personal-loan platform by managed AUM, profitable and scaling fast. But every rupee of the Rs.750 crore fresh issue goes into taking on more unsecured credit risk (DLG guarantees and NBFC capital) just as Stage 3 loans have nearly tripled, so this is one to track through a credit cycle rather than buy blind.

A profitable, export-heavy (95%) Madhya Pradesh maker of propeller shafts and driveline parts. About two-thirds of the fresh money goes into real capex and debt repayment. But revenue is growing only about 6% a year, part of the FY26 profit jump came from currency, half of product sales go to a US market under a 25% tariff, and the promoter-group governance record is weak. Our call is avoid at the IPO.

An Ahmedabad hardware system integrator for Gujarat and Maharashtra government schools and PSUs, now pivoting to solar EPC. It is raising a Rs.300 crore fresh issue, mainly to park as fixed deposits behind bank guarantees. The business has thin margins, heavy working capital and no visible moat, and there are several governance flags.

India's largest institutional on-campus student-housing operator is a real business with a scale lead, but this Rs 2,100 crore all-fresh issue mostly pays for promoter-group school assets (Rs 1,100 crore) and debt repayment (Rs 750 crore). Its FY26 profit jump rests on a one-off gain, it carries heavy leverage, and occupancy is falling. For a retail applicant the issue looks more like the promoter cashing out than new capital for the business.

A fast-growing Jaipur power-distribution EPC contractor whose profits have not yet turned into cash. It has no real moat and depends almost entirely on state discoms. Most of the new money will fund receivables and retention money, not new capacity. Worth tracking after listing, not applying to today.

A top-tier Morbi tile maker with a genuinely premium product mix (GVT and technical products are 84.19% of tile revenue) and a 3,000-plus outlet franchise network, raising Rs.320 crore of fresh money almost entirely to pay down debt while Carlyle's Katsura Investments takes Rs.388 crore off the table (S1) (S17) (S9).

A 21-station Auto LPG retailer in Telangana, Karnataka and Maharashtra raising ~Rs 50.75 crore of all-fresh money to add stations and cut debt -- genuinely profitable and growing, but selling a fuel that India has barely grown in a decade, with 99.75% of its gas from three suppliers and its trucking done by a promoter-owned company (S1)(S3)(S14).
